project.title: Beyond the Grasp: Occlusion and Failure Recovery
project.role: Project goals and task discussions, hands-on testing and failure feedback, requirements for comparisons, and learning Python and control code. Implementation, debugging and experiment preparation used AI assistance.
project.summary: A red object covers a blue target. The arm has to put the blue object in the bin and leave the red one out. Sometimes it extracts the target directly; sometimes it picks up the wrong object. I wanted the program to check what it actually holds before placing it—and recover when it gets that wrong.
project.tools: Isaac Sim, Isaac Lab, Python, RGB-D

detail.overview: A red object covers a blue target. The arm has to put the blue object in the bin and leave the red one out. Sometimes it extracts the target directly; sometimes it picks up the wrong object. I wanted the program to check what it actually holds before placing it—and recover when it gets that wrong.
detail.workflowNotes: The first extraction picks up the red object. After checking it, the program places it in the green staging area, locates the blue target again, and puts it in the bin. One complete 18.20-second episode, uncut from a fixed camera at the original simulation speed. Motion and recovery decisions are programmed.
challenges: So far, this has only been tested in simulation with known colors and object sizes, a fixed table and calibrated camera positions. Unfamiliar objects, complex terrain and real hardware remain untested.
The seven reported layouts form the development evaluation set. Generalisation to other layouts and collision behaviour require separate evaluation; the completion rate here applies to this set.
The next step is to hold the program fixed and compare it on layouts not used during debugging before deciding whether to extend the learned selector.

breakdown.label: Why the task changed
breakdown.text: An early demonstration pushed a red cube aside before grasping a blue one. But did the red cube really block the grasp? Would a different approach work directly? Comparisons showed that some layouts could indeed be solved without moving the obstacle. The task then changed to a red object covering the blue target: how can the robot extract the object underneath, and what should it do after grasping the wrong one?
bullets: Color and depth images locate the objects. Preset side views help locate the blue target when it is hidden from above.
After lifting, checks examine color and whether the object moves with the gripper. A verified red payload triggers staging and another grasp; insufficient evidence causes a stop.
Completion requires the blue target in the correct bin, the red object outside it, and both objects within the worktable area.

breakdown.label: When extraction works directly
breakdown.text: Here, the arm extracts the blue target from the side, checks it, and places it in the bin without recovery. The red object stays on the table. Both recordings use the same program and repeat existing development scenes; they add no new independent test samples.

media.note: 12.44 seconds · fixed camera · uncut at original simulation speed

breakdown.label: Results so far
breakdown.text: On seven layouts repeatedly used during debugging, both the current workflow and a relocate-first baseline completed all seven tasks. Of the six stacked layouts, two finished through direct extraction and four required recovery after acquiring the red object. Mean task times were 14.64 and 14.32 seconds, including failed attempts and recovery. The current workflow is not faster. It still needs checking on layouts that were not used for debugging.

cells: Move red first, then grasp blue

breakdown.label: A separate learning experiment
breakdown.text: I also explored reinforcement learning with a small neural network, using trial and feedback in simulation to learn when to grasp directly, approach diagonally, or move the red object first. Basic motions remained programmed. This separate PPO experiment ran for 96 training episodes, with 72 training-time completions. On the same twelve new development-validation scenes, the trained model and rules each completed ten tasks. The model averaged 12.51 seconds, versus 11.03 for rules, so it did not improve performance. It did not use the extraction-and-recovery program shown in the current videos; these results are reported separately.

breakdown.label: My part in the project
breakdown.text: I direct the task design and evaluation, using simulation runs to assess grasp strategies, identify failure patterns and set priorities for the next iteration. My work connects the project goals with concrete comparisons and observable results.
bullets: Reported specific failures: a closed gripper holding nothing, transport after an empty grasp, missing retries and premature scene resets. I supplied screenshots and logs and took part in discussions about checking what the gripper actually held.

Evaluated obstacle handling and alternative grasp directions. I identified opportunities to grasp directly rather than clear the obstacle first, driving strategy comparisons and a stacked-object task that tests extraction and recovery.

Asked for meaningful comparisons: camera-based localisation rather than presenting simulator object coordinates as vision; learned policies compared with fixed rules; and attention to time and failures as well as successful demonstrations.
Took part in choosing approaches and reviewing results, while learning Python, reading experiment reports and working through visual-coordinate, grasp-checking and control code.
breakdown.closingText: AI assisted with implementation, refactoring, debugging and experiment automation. I directed the task requirements, testing priorities and result review.

history.label: 2026-10-21 / Franka: Clearing the Way to Grasp a Target
history.text: I built a tabletop task in Isaac Sim: a robot arm has to put a blue cube into a bin, while a red cube sometimes blocks the grasp. I wanted to find out when the robot should grasp directly, push the obstacle aside, or move it elsewhere—and whether a trained policy could do better than fixed rules. Not yet. The rules select actions using predefined conditions; the models learn their choices through training. I compared fixed rules, the first model and V2 on the same six new scenes. All three completed all six tasks. V2 averaged about 1.36 seconds faster than the previous model, but was still about 1.22 seconds slower than the rules. The times measure task execution inside the simulation, excluding software startup. Six scenes are too few to establish reliability in other settings.

history.label: Early grasp checks
history.text: The project began with red and blue cube sorting. Empty grasps sometimes led to transport attempts, so visual checks were added after lifting to confirm that a cube moved with the gripper.

history.label: V0.17: Sorting trials
history.text: The earlier controller completed 16 sorting batches and correctly placed 63 cubes. Two separate camera-failure cases stopped as intended. These sorting results are recorded separately from the current obstacle task.

history.label: V0.18: Nearby cubes
history.text: A separate perception experiment examined nearby or touching same-color cubes. Ten supported layouts had localization errors below 5 mm, with a maximum of about 1.71 mm. Two other layouts could not be identified reliably. This used a known 40 mm cube-size assumption and was not yet connected to dense grasping.
